thread.title: Dow Rises 91 Points Because Everybody's Ready for a New Year

title: Dow Rises 91 Points Because Everybody's Ready for a New Year
text:
Dow Rises 91 Points Because Everybody’s Ready for a New Year By Dec. 31, 2018 11:42 a.m. ET Order Reprints Michael Haddad Text size
Long December . After a turbulent fourth quarter and the worst December since 1931, stocks were trading up on the last day of 2018, as investors hope for a better year ahead. In today’s Intraday Update , we… look back at a tumultuous year; feel hopeful about 2019; and see what’s boosting Crispr Therapeutics (CRSP).
Don’t Look Back in Anger
Markets may be firmly lodged in the red for 2018, but stocks are ending 2018 on an upbeat note, with all three indexes moderately by midday Monday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 91.13, or 0.40%, to 23,153.53. The S&P 500 is up 0.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite is edging 0.1% higher.
It’s been a fairly quiet end to the year, as is often the case. A tweet by President Donald Trump over the weekend, saying that the U.S. and China had made “big progress” in trade talks, however, may be contributing to the celebratory mood. Recent rallies mean that the last five trading days of the year have been the best since 2008 for the S&P and the Dow, and the Nasdaq’s best year-end since 2000.
So while we had no Santa rally, plenty of investors are anticipating the start of a robust January effect.
Year to date through Friday, only two of the S&P’s 11 sectors posted gains, but “history divines an encouraging implication from these negative returns,” writes CFRA’s Sam Stovall. Since 1970, the S&P 500 recorded an average annual total return of 11.6% and was up 80% of the time, and during this period, the best- and worst-performing sectors differed by 41 percentage points. That compares to just a 23.5 point difference between health care and energy, 2018’s biggest winner and loser. “In the year after recording a below-average differential, the S&P 500 posted a positive full-year total return 91% of the time…So should history repeat, and there’s no guarantee it will, this year’s lump of coal could metamorphize into an unanticipated gem.”
There are no guarantees, in life or stocks, but after a brutal December, any encouragement is welcome. Yet as investors tiptoe back into the market in the last few days, they’re following the lead of corporate insiders: “One recent bright spot has been insider buying,” writes James Investment Research’s Matt Watson. Executives stepped up their buying in the fourth quarter amid stock-market swoons, and corporations “set a new record in 2018 for the amount of stock they repurchased,” which amounted to nearly $600 billion in the first three quarters.
That may be cold comfort at the moment—after all, as Watson notes, Apple (AAPL) is in an $11 billion hole with the shares it bought back this year—but at least managements are putting their money where their mouths are.
Plus, despite all the doom and gloom in markets recently, there’s still fundamental reason for optimism. “Corrections tend to be an indication of investors pricing rising risks into asset prices but tend not to be predictive of whether those risks will materialize or persist,” writes Glenmede’s Jason Pride. Investors will want reassurance that the economy and corporate earnings are still healthier than recent selloffs have indicated, but his firm sees just a 36% chance of recession ahead, suggesting a “continuation of the expansion is more likely.”
Perhaps December’s best lesson is that—to not get caught up in fear, and try to stick with facts. And a little more optimism is never a bad new year’s resolution.
Midday Movers
American Midstream Partners (AMID) is down 32.8% to $2.91 after disclosing an amendment to its credit agreement and saying that it does not expect to make any cash distributions on its common units or preferred units with in the fourth quarter.
Camping World Holdings (CWH) is down 7.5% to $11.48 after disclosing in a regulatory filing that the president of its Camping World and FreedomRoads divisions resigned, effective immediately, on December 21.
Crispr Therapeutics is up 6.8% to $25.58 after Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX), up 1.9% to $164.43, increased its active stake to 10.4% from 10.29%.
Heron Therapeutics (HRTX) is up 5.8% to $25.12 after the Food and Drug Administration granted priority review of its pain relief opioid alternative.
Sun Life Financial (SLF) is up 1.6% to $33.09 after Argus upgraded it to Buy.
